subtitle: Data science is a loop, not a line: ask, collect, clean, explore, model, check, deploy, and go round again.

what.body:
Every time a streaming app guesses your next favourite show, or a hospital spots a patient at risk before anyone notices, someone has turned a pile of data into a decision. That is the craft you are about to learn.

Data science extracts knowledge and decisions from data using statistics, programming and domain understanding. It sits where three skills meet: mathematics/statistics (what is true?), computing (how do we do it at scale?) and the domain (is it meaningful?). Take away any one and the whole thing wobbles like a three-legged stool.

You will hear some cousin terms, so let’s sort them out. Analytics describes the past. Machine learning learns patterns to predict. Big data means volume, velocity and variety beyond one machine. So what is the aim of data science? To turn data into knowledge and better decisions.
keynotes: Data science extracts knowledge and decisions from data using statistics, programming and domain understanding.
It sits between mathematics/statistics (what is true?), computing (at scale?) and the domain (is it meaningful?).
Analytics describes the past, machine learning learns patterns to predict, and big data means volume, velocity and variety beyond one machine.

loop.body:
Here is the first surprise: data science is not a straight road from question to answer. It is a loop. The typical stages (CRISP-DM style) run business understanding → data collection → preparation → exploration → modeling → evaluation → deployment → monitoring.

But results at any stage often send you back. Poor evaluation means you revisit the features or collect more data, like a chef who tastes the soup and goes back to the spice rack. Follow the arrows in the figure, and see the “not yet” arrow: that is the loop. If your model scores badly, where do you go? Back, of course, not forward.
keynotes: Stages: business understanding, data collection, preparation, exploration, modeling, evaluation, deployment, monitoring.
Results at any stage often send you back.
Poor evaluation means revisiting features or collecting more data.

types.body:
Not all data looks alike, and the shape of your data decides what you can do with it. Here are the three big families.

KindExamples
Structuredtables, SQL rows
Semi-structuredJSON, XML, logs
Unstructuredtext, images, audio

Inside a table, variables are numeric (discrete or continuous) or categorical (nominal, or ordinal if ordered). The type decides which summary and chart are allowed: you can average ages but not colours. Is “small, medium, large” nominal or ordinal? It has an order, so it is ordinal.
keynotes: Structured data is tables and SQL rows; semi-structured is JSON, XML and logs; unstructured is text, images and audio.
Variables are numeric (discrete or continuous) or categorical (nominal, or ordinal if ordered).
The type decides which summary and chart are allowed.

roles.body:
Where does data actually come from, and who handles it? Sources include databases, APIs, sensors/IoT, web scraping, surveys and logs. Sensor readings streaming from a machine are a perfect example of IoT data.

The usual tools are Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn), SQL, notebooks and visualisation libraries. And it takes a team: data engineers build pipelines, analysts explain, and scientists model. You will wear all three hats at some point.
keynotes: Sources: databases, APIs, sensors/IoT, web scraping, surveys and logs.
Typical tools: Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn), SQL, notebooks and visualisation libraries.
Data engineers build pipelines, analysts explain and scientists model.

bias.body:
A manager says, “improve sales.” Where do you even begin? A vague goal like that has to become a measurable question, such as “which customers will churn in 30 days?”. Good questions come before any code.

Then comes the sample, and here is a warning you will thank me for later: a random sample represents the population; convenience or self-selected samples are biased. More data does not fix a biased sample. A bigger crowd of the wrong people is still the wrong people. An online poll answered only by people who chose to click is a self-selected sample.

One more trap. A shop has 400 customers and 60 churned last month, a churn rate of 60/400 = 0.15. Predicting “no churn” for everyone is right 85 % of the time, yet useless, because accuracy alone misleads on imbalanced data.
keynotes: A vague goal such as “improve sales” becomes a measurable question such as “which customers will churn in 30 days?”.
A random sample represents the population; convenience or self-selected samples are biased, and more data does not fix that.
With 60 of 400 customers churning (0.15), predicting no churn for everyone is right 85 % of the time yet useless.

lim.body:
Data is powerful, but it is not magic, and an honest scientist knows where the edges are. Correlation is not causation: ice-cream sales and sunburn rise together, yet ice cream does not burn you. Past patterns may not hold tomorrow. And a model is only as good as its data: garbage in, garbage out.

So how do you earn a causal claim? With a randomised experiment, an A/B test, where chance alone decides who gets which treatment. That is the design that best supports a causal claim.
keynotes: Correlation is not causation, and past patterns may not hold.
A model is only as good as its data: garbage in, garbage out.
Randomised experiments (A/B tests) are how causal claims are earned.
